title: Errors and Result
intro: A function that can fail returns `Result<T, E>`: either `Ok(value)` or `Err(error)`. The `?` operator means "if this failed, return the error right now", in one character.

coming_from.go: `Result<T, E>` replaces `(T, error)`, and `?` does what `if err != nil { return err }` does. Go is the closest cousin: errors are plain values that you return and check. The difference is that Rust won't hand you the value until you have dealt with the `Err` case, and warns when you ignore a `Result` altogether.
coming_from.kotlin: Expected failures are return values, not exceptions: `Result<T, E>` is a bit like Kotlin's `Result` from `runCatching`, but the error type is spelled out (Kotlin's is always a `Throwable`). `?` passes the error up to the caller, and there is no `try`/`catch` for expected failures. Rust keeps panics for bugs.
coming_from.python: There is no `try`/`except` for normal failures: the function returns `Result<T, E>`, either `Ok(value)` or `Err(error)`. `?` passes the error up the way an exception you don't catch would, but the possibility of failure shows in the function's type.
coming_from.typescript: There is no `throw`/`catch` for normal failures. A `Result<T, E>` is like returning a union of `{ ok: true, value }` and `{ ok: false, error }`, but it is built in, so the standard library and crates share the same one. The error type is in the signature (in strict mode a `catch` variable is `unknown`), and `?` passes it up.
coming_from.java: `Result<T, E>` is a return value, not an exception, so the error shows up in the signature like a checked exception but travels like normal data. `?` means "return the error to my caller now", which is what an uncaught checked exception does when your method declares `throws`.
coming_from.csharp: Rust has no exceptions for normal errors: a function returns `Result<T, E>`, either `Ok` or `Err`. It's like the `TryParse` pattern built into the type system, and `?` passes the error up to the caller in one character.
coming_from.c: `Result<T, E>` is C's "return an error code and write the value through a pointer", packed into one value. The compiler won't let you use the value without dealing with the error, and `?` is the `if (err) return err;` line.
coming_from.cpp: `Result<T, E>` replaces throwing: the error is part of the return type, and `?` returns it early instead of unwinding. C++20's standard library has no equivalent; C++23's `std::expected` is the same idea.

notes: Expected failures are ordinary return values, not exceptions, and the compiler won't let you use the value without dealing with the error. A `panic!` is the other kind of failure: it is for bugs, and it ends the thread it happens on (on the main thread, the program).
`?` only works inside a function whose return type can carry the error: `Result` for a `Result`, `Option` for an `Option`. In `main`, write `-> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>>` to use it.
In real projects, the `thiserror` and `anyhow` crates (add-on libraries) remove most of the boilerplate: see [Errors in real apps](/build/app-errors/).

gotcha.title: A Result is not the value
gotcha.looks_fine: Most languages let you use the number right away: `int("42") + 1` in Python, `Integer.parseInt("42") + 1` in Java, or in Go `n, _ := strconv.Atoi("42")`, which names the error and throws it away. For the text "42" that is fine, because you can see it is a number.
gotcha.rust_sees: `parse` returns `Result<u32, ...>`, not a `u32`. The compiler does not look at the text "42". It only knows that parsing text can fail.
gotcha.why: The same line with a user's input could get "abc". Rust makes you choose what happens on failure. `.unwrap_or(0)` means "use 0 if it fails" on purpose (the same as Go's `_`), `?` means "pass the error to my caller", and `.unwrap()` means "stop if wrong", which is what an uncaught exception does elsewhere, minus the stack trace.

go.says: Go runs this and prints 43. The `_` is written out, so ignoring the error is a visible choice, and for "42" it does no harm. With "abc" the error is thrown away, `n` is 0, and the program quietly prints 1.

kotlin.says: Kotlin runs this and prints 43. With "abc", `toInt()` would throw a NumberFormatException, and nothing in the code warns you.

python.says: Python prints 43. `int("42")` works, and if the text were "abc" it would raise a ValueError you didn't catch.

typescript.says: Prints 43. `parseInt` never throws: bad input like "abc" gives `NaN`, and the math carries on with it.

java.says: This prints 43. NumberFormatException is unchecked, so nothing makes you handle it; with "abc" the same line would throw at runtime.

csharp.says: `uint.Parse` hands back the number directly and prints 43. A bad string would throw a FormatException, which nothing here catches.

c.says: `atoi` has no way to report an error. It gives 42 for "42", but it also turns "abc" into 0, so the second number is a wrong 1.

cpp.says: `std::stoi` hands back the number directly and prints 43. A bad input would throw an exception, but nothing in the types makes you handle it.
